briefEdits.from: The court recognized substantial immunity in appropriate circumstances. In *Whited v. Phillips*, a nonresident voluntarily came to answer an indictment; immunity protected his attendance. In *Morris v. Calhoun*, a person appeared in another county pursuant to a public-safety officer’s citation. In *Lang v. Shaw*, a person returned to the county to answer a criminal charge after release on recognizance. These examples connect the person’s presence to responding to judicial or equivalent criminal process. By contrast, *State ex rel. Godby v. Chambers* refused immunity to a person already serving a misdemeanor sentence: confinement did not itself constitute the kind of criminal process that justified the privilege. Id. at 115.

briefEdits.from: Does a Sherman Act § 1 complaint state a claim under Rule 8(a)(2) when it alleges parallel anticompetitive behavior and a conclusory agreement, without factual context plausibly suggesting that the defendants acted pursuant to an agreement? Rule and Holding A complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to make entitlement to relief plausible. Detailed evidentiary pleading is unnecessary, and plausibility is not a requirement to show that liability is more likely than not. For a § 1 conspiracy claim, however, the pleaded circumstances must suggest agreement and give a reasonable expectation that discovery will reveal evidence of it. Parallel conduct plus an unsupported assertion of conspiracy does not satisfy that requirement. Opinion of the Court, pt. II.B; CB pp. 619–620.

# Peacock Construction Co. v. Modern Air Conditioning, Inc.
353 So. 2d 840 (Fla. 1977) | Decided December 15, 1977 | Contracts

## Completed subcontracts and an unpaid owner
Peacock was the general contractor on a condominium project. Modern Air Conditioning undertook the heating and air conditioning work, while Overly Manufacturing undertook the rooftop swimming pool work. Each written subcontract placed final payment within thirty days after completion, written architectural acceptance, and full payment by the owner. The subcontractors completed their work and requested payment. No deficiencies had been found; in Modern’s case the architect testified under oath that the equipment, though not yet operated, was complete according to the plans and specifications. Peacock had not received full payment from the owner, a corporation that entered bankruptcy proceedings. 353 So. 2d at 841 & nn.2–4.

The owner’s failure to pay made the clause’s interpretation decisive. If owner payment was a condition of Peacock’s duty, the subcontractors bore the owner’s nonpayment risk even after completing their work. If it instead specified timing for an unconditional payment promise, the subcontractors could recover after a reasonable period. The case involved that allocation of risk, not a dispute over defective subcontractor performance.

## Two judgments and conflicting appellate approaches
Modern and Overly brought separate breach actions in the Lee County Circuit Court. The trial judges granted summary judgment to each, implicitly rejecting owner payment as a condition precedent. The Second District affirmed Modern’s judgment, following the prevailing approach that clauses of this kind constitute absolute promises to pay and identify a reasonable payment time. It then affirmed Overly on Modern’s authority. Id. at 841–42 & nn.5–7.

The Florida Supreme Court accepted conflict certiorari and consolidated the two causes for appellate purposes. In Gerrits, the Third District had reversed a subcontractor’s summary judgment under similar payment language because intent should be resolved by a jury once the general contractor raised it. Peacock asked the Supreme Court to adopt that approach. It conceded the weight of contrary authority but argued that the parties first deserved an opportunity to offer evidence on intent. Only if no evidence supported a condition should the judge direct a verdict for the subcontractors. Id. at 841 n.1, 842.

## Judicial interpretation of the ambiguous payment language
The court acknowledged that the provisions could be read either as conditions precedent or as a means of fixing a reasonable payment time. Its choice did not depend on declaring the text incapable of the contractor’s proposed reading. Instead, the court treated interpretation as a question of law when the transaction’s familiar nature permitted the parties’ ordinary intent to be determined judicially. It recognized that the meaning of language has a factual dimension, but rejected Peacock’s contention that this ambiguity necessarily required a jury trial. Id. at 842.

Small subcontractors on large projects ordinarily need payment to stay in business and do not intend to accept the risk that the owner will fail to pay the general contractor. That recurring commercial relationship supported construing ambiguous owner-payment provisions as unconditional promises with payment due within a reasonable time. The court joined the majority approach, whose supporting and contrary authorities appear in footnote 6. Id. at 841–42 & nn.6, 8. This avoided converting ordinary timing language into an insolvency-risk transfer merely because the owner’s receipt of funds was listed in the clause.

## Express risk shifting remains possible
The court expressly preserved the parties’ ability to allocate owner nonpayment risk to a subcontractor. Such a transfer must be unambiguously expressed, and the general contractor bears the burden of clear expression. The opinion therefore does not invalidate every agreement making payment conditional or guarantee recovery regardless of contractual language. It decides the treatment of ambiguous final-payment provisions in this construction relationship. Id. at 842–43.

Neither a precise new due date nor a general test for every kind of contractual ambiguity was announced. The important distinction is between an agreed condition shifting the risk of permanent nonpayment and language regulating the time for an otherwise absolute debt. Because these subcontracts did not clearly make the subcontractors bear the risk, the judgments did not depend on the bankrupt owner eventually paying Peacock.

## Judgment and participation
The Supreme Court adopted the Second District’s two decisions as controlling Florida law and overruled Gerrits to the extent inconsistent. It discharged the orders allowing certiorari, leaving both favorable summary judgments undisturbed. Boyd, acting chief justice, wrote; England, Sundberg, Hatchett, and Karl concurred. Five judges participated as listed, and no separate writing is reported. Id. at 843.

## Reading scope and limits
The complete judicial text, all eight footnotes, and the entire assigned principal excerpt were read. The casebook retains the owner-bankruptcy note but renumbers it as footnote 1; it corresponds to the complete opinion’s footnote 4. Later editorial discussion following NOTES is not part of the judgment. The accompanying author record archives the reporter reproduction and checked page markers. This brief states the 1977 holding; subsequent statutory or judicial treatment was not assessed with a citator.

# Peacock Construction Co. v. Modern Air Conditioning, Inc.
353 So. 2d 840 (Fla. 1977) | Decided December 15, 1977 | Contracts

## Who had to pay whom?
Peacock was the general contractor on a condominium project. It hired Modern Air Conditioning for the heating and air conditioning work, and Overly Manufacturing for the rooftop swimming pool work. Each subcontract made final payment due within thirty days after completion, the architect's written acceptance, and full payment by the owner. Both subcontractors completed their work and requested payment. No defects had been found. The architect testified under oath that Modern's equipment met the plans and specifications, although it had not yet been operated. The owner had not paid Peacock in full and had entered bankruptcy proceedings. 353 So. 2d at 841 & nn.2–4.

There were two ways to read the payment clause. One would make the owner's payment a condition of Peacock's duty: if the owner never paid, the subcontractors would bear that loss. The other would treat the clause as setting the time for a debt Peacock still owed. On that reading, payment would become due after a reasonable time even if the owner never paid. The dispute concerned this risk, not defective work.

## How the cases reached the Supreme Court
Modern and Overly sued separately in the Lee County Circuit Court. Each trial judge granted summary judgment, deciding that the subcontractor could recover without a trial. Those rulings necessarily rejected Peacock's argument that the owner's payment was a condition precedent to its duty to pay. The Second District affirmed Modern's judgment, treating the clause as an unconditional promise with a reasonable time for payment. It then affirmed Overly's judgment by following Modern's case. Id. at 841–42 & nn.5–7.

The Florida Supreme Court accepted review through conflict certiorari, a procedure for resolving conflicting decisions of Florida appeals courts, and considered the cases together. In Gerrits, the Third District had set aside a subcontractor's summary judgment under similar language. It had said that a jury should resolve intent once the general contractor raised that factual issue. Peacock urged the Supreme Court to follow Gerrits. It acknowledged that most courts took the other view, but wanted a chance to offer evidence of intent. Peacock argued that the judge should direct a verdict for the subcontractors only if no evidence supported a condition. Id. at 841 n.1, 842.

## Why the judge could interpret the unclear clause
The Supreme Court accepted that the clauses could bear either meaning. It did not pretend that Peacock's reading was impossible. But an ambiguity did not automatically require a jury. Judges generally interpret written contracts as a question of law when the nature of the transaction lets them identify the parties' ordinary intent. The court recognized that language also has a factual dimension, but rejected Peacock's claim that this uncertainty necessarily required a trial. Id. at 842.

The recurring business relationship supplied the answer. Small subcontractors need payment for their work to stay in business. They ordinarily do not agree to take the risk that the project owner will fail to pay the general contractor. The court therefore joined the majority approach: unclear clauses of this kind are promises to pay within a reasonable time. The supporting and contrary authorities appear in footnote 6. Id. at 841–42 & nn.6, 8.

Merely listing the owner's payment as a step before final payment did not clearly transfer the risk of the owner's insolvency. Because these clauses did not clearly make the subcontractors bear that risk, their judgments did not depend on the bankrupt owner eventually paying Peacock.

## A clearly written condition could produce a different result
The court expressly allowed parties to agree that the subcontractor would bear the owner's nonpayment risk. But that intention had to be stated unambiguously, and the general contractor had the burden of making it clear. The decision did not invalidate all conditional-payment agreements or guarantee payment regardless of the contract's wording. Id. at 842–43.

The distinction is between a condition that shifts the risk of permanent nonpayment and a timing clause for money that is still owed. The court did not announce a precise new due date or a rule for resolving every contractual ambiguity. It decided the effect of unclear final-payment clauses in this construction relationship.

## Result and judges
The Supreme Court adopted the Second District's decisions as controlling Florida law and overruled Gerrits to the extent it conflicted. It discharged the orders allowing certiorari, leaving both summary judgments for the subcontractors in place. Boyd, acting chief justice, wrote the opinion. England, Sundberg, Hatchett, and Karl concurred. Five judges participated as listed, and no separate opinion is reported. Id. at 843.
